source: MAFF General Directorate of Agriculture, បច្ចេកទេសដាំដុះដំណាំចេក (Techniques for Banana Cultivation), 2019, section I.1 (អំពីផ្រវត្តិ)
text:
Banana (ចេក) is believed to have originated in the Southeast Asian archipelago region, with cultivation dating back roughly to 1400 BC, from where it later spread to Africa. From there, traders and travelers carried the crop further, and by the 16th century two varieties known as Silk Fig and French Plantain had become the dominant types carried to new regions and colonies. In the 19th century, breeding and selection work produced other well-known varieties, most notably Gros Michel (known locally by a name meaning "golden ambong"), which became a major commercial variety worldwide, though it was later devastated by Panama disease (Fusarium wilt), which forced growers in many countries to abandon it in favor of more resistant types. The Cavendish group, which dominates the global export trade today, rose to prominence afterward largely because of its resistance to the strain of Panama disease that wiped out Gros Michel plantations.

In Cambodia specifically, organized banana cultivation is understood to have expanded significantly from around 1964 onward. Long-standing local varieties grown by Cambodian farmers include Chek Mean Krob (seeded/wild-type banana), Chek Ambong, and Chek Ambong Khmer. Chek Ambong Khmer in particular has a long history of being grown in provincial areas and in home gardens, and different regional populations of it show some variation in bunch and fruit characteristics.

Today banana is grown across most of the world's tropical and subtropical regions, with especially large production in Asia and Africa, and it remains one of the most widely consumed and traded fruit crops globally.
